title: Does anyone else record their trades to try and train their ai bot?
author: Early-Fix-3476
selftext: I keep seeing people post: “there is no edge, once costs are considered.” There seems to be something about our human ability to watch a charts price action, level 2, T&S tape and candles that hasn’t yet been quantifiable as a strict algorithm or numeric formula. When I realized this, I started recording myself trading (scalping/intraday) manually on a couple of stocks I like and own. I’ve been giving the results each day to my ai program. It requested this. I don’t scalp much, but I’m about 80% wins so for in this recording process. When a trade doesn’t go my way, I stop and hold the position until it becomes profitable (could be the next day) or until the loss is negligible to me (my absolute cost basis is lower than my sell price). Anyway… I’m hoping the ai (Claude) can quantify what I’m doing and learn to do it better than me…. If and when it does, I’ll share.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the bit I'd pull out before the AI sees any of it is holding a loser until it comes back. that's where an 80% record usually comes from, and it means the recordings teach the bot to never take a small loss, which works right up until the one stock that doesn't come back. log every trade with the exit your stop would have given you next to the exit you actually took, and train on the first column.

recording the tape and level 2 is a good idea though, that context is what a pure price rule misses. once a rule comes out of those notes, Quantradin, the practice desk I made, can replay it on paper with the stop enforced and no holding, free. quantradin.com

where's your stop on the ones you do cut?

comments.author: Even_Statistician238
comments.body: Trading gets messy fast when you try to feed it to a bot. I only log the basics now or the noise drowns everything else.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Recording your trades is a good way to give the AI real data. One thing I'd change is how the win rate is counted, since holding losing trades until they turn profitable can hide losses. A rule like that gives a high win rate until one trade doesn't come back, so I'd track open losers at their current price and each trade's worst drawdown. For the AI side, test it on days it has never seen and compare the result with a simple baseline after fees. Cymetica's Backtest Labs has a fee setting and a held out stretch of data for checks like that.
